title: Sales Enablement: Enterprise Playbook — Positioning, Competitive Briefs, Pitch Decks, Pricing Guidance, Case Studies & Security FAQ
author: Liam Patel
body:
Purpose

This playbook is a single-source, prospect-facing reference for Redwood Inference sellers and solutions engineers. It consolidates positioning and messaging, competitive briefs, a recommended pitch-deck flow, pricing guidance, representative case studies, and a concise security FAQ tailored for enterprise prospects evaluating inference platforms. Use this during discovery, technical meetings, and procurement conversations.

Executive summary

- Elevator pitch: Redwood Inference is a developer-first inference platform that makes LLM-powered applications predictable, economical, and reliable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Core wins: consistent latency and throughput guarantees, unified workflow across deployment modes, cost-performance controls (batching, caching, quantization), and enterprise-grade security/compliance.
- Primary targets: platform & ML teams at AI-native startups, product teams at mid-market/enterprise companies, and centralized platform/infra teams responsible for LLM adoption.

1) Positioning & messaging

Target personas and messages
- ML Engineer / Model Ops: "Deploy and scale model inference with predictable latency and token costs; keep outputs consistent across environments."
- Backend/Platform Engineer: "A single API and runtime that maps to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — simplifies ops and reduces fragmentation."
- Security/Compliance: "Private deployment options, control-plane separation, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, and per-route data residency controls."
- Product Manager / Line-of-Business: "Ship LLM features faster with measurable unit economics and guardrails to maintain quality as models change."

Top-level value propositions
- Production-first throughput & latency: SLOs and observability for token-level latency/cost accountability.
- Unified developer experience: same API/SDK and rollout tools across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Cost & performance controls: intelligent batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization suggestions to reduce per-token cost.
- Reliability & graceful degradation: model variants, regional fallback, and automatic retries to protect SLAs.

Proof points & one-liners
- "Reduce per-token inference cost by up to 3x with batching + caching while maintaining 99th percentile latency targets."
- "Trusted by customers in regulated industries with VPC and on-prem private deployments and KMS integrations."

2) Competitive brief (short)

Key competitors to position against
- Vendor A (Large managed LLM API): Easiest to get started but limited on private deployment and limited batching control. Use when speed of experiments > production economics.
- Vendor B (Cloud-hosted model endpoints): Strong in infra scale but weaker on inference-specific kernel optimizations and unified rollout tooling across private/on-prem.
- Vendor C (Open-source self-hosted runtimes): Excellent control and cost on paper but requires significant platform investment and lacks managed observability & canary rollouts.

How Redwood wins (differentiators to emphasize)
- Unified runtime + orchestration: same APIs and rollout controls across hosted, dedicated, and private.
- Observability tied to costs: token-level cost breakdowns, per-route SLOs, and regression alerts tied to evals.
- Production kernel & scheduling optimizations: lower latency at scale with continuous batching and KV cache awareness.
- Enterprise controls: reserved capacity, SLA-backed latency/uptime, KMS/HSM + audit logging, and private control plane options.

Competitive objection handling (short examples)
- "We already use managed API X": Ask about production pain (cost surprises, latency spikes, or failed rollouts). Show token-level cost breakdown and a sample optimization plan.
- "We self-host to save costs": Clarify total cost of ownership (ops, reliability, feature gaps like rollouts/observability). Offer a Dedicated evaluation (reserved pool + SRE support) or Private POC.

3) Pitch deck: recommended flow and slide-by-slide bullets

Slide 1 — Title + One-liner
- Company + presenter, quick one-line: "High-performance LLM inference with predictable economics and enterprise controls."

Slide 2 — Why now
- Rapid adoption of LLM features; models and hardware changing faster than teams can manage; cost and reliability are the gating factors.

Slide 3 — Customer problem
- Examples: token-cost surprises, latency variability, inconsistent behavior between dev/staging/prod, difficulty running private deployments.

Slide 4 — Solution overview
- Redwood platform overview (hosted, dedicated, private). Key capabilities: runtime, caching, batch tuning, rollout controls, observability.

Slide 5 — Architecture diagram
- High-level diagram showing client apps -> Redwood API -> smart router -> serving runtime -> (hosted/dedicated/private). Call out KV-cache, batching layer, and model variants.

Slide 6 — Performance & cost examples
- Benchmarks: 95th/99th latency targets, per-token cost reductions from batching & quantization, sample throughput for medium/large models.

Slide 7 — Security & compliance
- Private control plane, VPC/peering, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logging, SOC/ISO evidence (if available).

Slide 8 — Pricing options (summary)
- Hosted: pay-as-you-go per token + optional reserved credits.
- Dedicated: monthly reserved GPU capacity with predictable throughput.
- Private: licensing + support and optional deployment engineering.

Slide 9 — Roadmap & support
- Integrations (customer plugins, evals, model onboarding), enterprise SLAs, professional services offerings.

Slide 10 — Case studies & outcomes
- Short callouts with metrics (latency, cost savings, time-to-production).

Slide 11 — Next steps & POC options
- Suggest a 4–6 week POC + success criteria (latency baseline, per-token cost target, rollout test).

4) Pricing guidance (discussion & negotiation playbook)

Pricing tiers (guidance)
- Hosted (self-serve): baseline per-token rates for generation and embeddings; usage tiers with volume discounts; enterprise add-ons for longer retention and higher SLA.
- Dedicated (reserved): monthly fee for reserved GPU pools. Pricing modeled on committed capacity (e.g., v100/A100-equivalent units) + overage or burst policies. Include a migration path from Hosted to Dedicated.
- Private: license + deployment & support fees. Optional annual support/maintenance.

Negotiation levers & best practices
- Commit horizon: increase discount for 12+ month commitments.
- Capacity commitments: customers that reserve baseline throughput receive preferred pricing.
- Bundling: observability retention, eval-run packs, and premium SLAs can be bundled for enterprise deals.
- Trial pricing: provide limited free credits for first 30 days and a pilot discount for customers willing to sign a pilot statement of work.

Sample pricing examples (illustrative numbers for sales use only)
- Small SaaS pilot: Hosted + $10k credits for 6 weeks; expected spend post-trial ~ $2k/mo.
- Mid-market: Dedicated small pool (equivalent to 2x A100) — $40k/mo committed with 10% discount for annual prepay.
- Enterprise private: $300k license + $100k first-year deployment & support (one-time).

Legal & procurement notes
- Typical contract items: data processing addendum (DPA), SOC/ISO evidence, SLAs tied to uptime/latency tiers, and limits on subprocessing. Include procurement path templates in related pages.

5) Case studies (short vignettes for prospects)

Case study A — Fintech fraud-detection assistant
- Customer profile: mid-market fintech with strict data residency requirements.
- Problem: latency spikes on peak days, high per-token costs from naive batching, inability to run models in a private network.
- Redwood solution: Private deployment with KMS, tuned batching, and KV caching; canary rollout to validate quality.
- Outcome: 2.5x reduction in per-token cost, 40% reduction in 99th percentile latency, full compliance with data residency and audit requirements.

Case study B — Retail personalization at scale
- Customer profile: large online retailer using embeddings for product recommendations.
- Problem: bursty traffic, inconsistent throughput on third-party endpoints, and cost unpredictability.
- Redwood solution: Dedicated reserved capacity with autoscaling policies and intelligent routing for regional fallbacks.
- Outcome: stable 99.9% availability, 30% lower inference cost vs prior provider (measured after batching & quantization), and simplified rollout process for model updates.

6) Security FAQ for prospects (concise answers; use in discovery and technical calls)

Q: Can Redwood run in our VPC/on-prem?
A: Yes. We support Private deployments (VPC and on-prem options) with a customer-managed control plane. For highly regulated customers we provide an on-prem appliance and deployment automation.

Q: How do you handle key management and encryption?
A: Redwood integrates with customer-managed KMS and supports HSM-backed key stores for private deployments. All data at-rest and in-transit is TLS encrypted; audit logs capture key events.

Q: Where does customer data reside?
A: Customers can choose region placement for the hosted control plane. For Private deployments, data and control-plane components are under customer network control. We provide configuration matrices for supported regions and residency.

Q: What compliance evidence is available?
A: We maintain SOC2-type evidence for hosted components and provide customer-specific compliance packages for Private deployments. Contact security-compliance@redwood.ai for the current artifacts and evidence process.

Q: How do you minimize model leakage or data retention risk?
A: We recommend and support per-route data handling policies, request-level redaction, and short retention windows for KV caches. Private deployments allow customers to avoid any control-plane data routing.

Q: Do you provide audit logging and traceability?
A: Yes. Audit logs include request metadata, model version, route, and token consumption. Logs can be exported to customer SIEMs or long-term storage.

Q: How are updates and rollouts handled securely?
A: Rollouts are controlled via canary and A/B policies in the Console; private deployment updates are performed through signed artifacts and gated by security reviews.

7) Sales playbook & discovery checklist

Discovery questions (technical + business)
- Who are the primary internal stakeholders (platform, security, product, procurement)?
- What are your latency & throughput targets (p50/p95/p99)?
- Do you have data residency or control-plane isolation requirements?
- What volume/seasonality do you expect? Are there predictable peaks?
- Current pain: cost surprises, rollout failures, model quality regressions, or poor observability?

POC / success criteria (example)
- Baseline measurement: p95/p99 latencies and cost per 10k tokens.
- Target: reduce p99 latency by X% and per-token cost by Y% within 6 weeks.
- Quality gate: no more than Z% regression on model eval prompt set.

Objection handling (short scripts)
- Cost: "Show me the math" — run a token-level cost model and share a sample optimization plan (batching, caching, quantization).
- Security: "Can we host inside our network?" — propose Private POC + KMS integration and reference prior deployments.

8) Enablement artifacts and templates (links and next steps)

- Sales deck template: use the slide flow above; keep decks under 12 slides for executive meetings.
- Technical demo checklist: live inference with p95/p99 metrics, cost breakdown, and rollout demo.
- POC SOW template: 4–6 week pilot, defined success criteria, resourcing expectations (solutions engineer + infra support).
- Pricing calculator: internal spreadsheet to estimate Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private economics (link in related pages).
